plan.assignment_rule: Meaning items: M2 if the target is a phrase or all options are phrases, else M1. Blank items: B6 if any option is multiword, else B5 if a negator frames the blank's sentence, else B1 to B4 by primary clue (report 7d; collocation and tone counted as restatement).

items.passage: Historian Marisa J. Fuentes’s Dispossessed Lives (2016) examines eighteenth-century Bridgetown, Barbados, through the experiences of enslaved women whose lives survive in the archive only in ______ form. Reading the brief mentions of these women in colonial records alongside Black feminist theory, Fuentes shows how the power of slave owners and officials shaped what those documents preserve.
items.stem: Which choice completes the text with the most logical and precise word or phrase?
items.explanation: The second sentence says Fuentes works from “brief mentions” of these women in colonial records. Lives that survive only as brief mentions survive in pieces, so the archive preserves them only in fragmentary form.

B.why_wrong: Comprehensive means complete, but the women appear only in brief mentions, the opposite of a full record.

C.why_wrong: The women appear in colonial records, which are documents, not fiction; nothing suggests the archive invents their lives.

D.why_wrong: Nothing says the records overstate the women’s lives; the problem described is how little the records say.

sources.what: Dispossessed Lives: Enslaved Women, Violence, and the Archive, Marisa J. Fuentes, University of Pennsylvania Press 2016 (Early American Studies); women whose stories appear only briefly in historical records; fragmentary sources combined with black feminist theory; power of slave owners, colonial authorities and the archive
Publisher description: in the eighteenth century Bridgetown, Barbados, was heavily populated by enslaved and free women; their stories appear only briefly in historical records

items.notes: Title italic in print. Theme: history (Caribbean slavery, archival method).
items.replaced: Jacob Lawrence, The Migration Series (duplicate of inferences.S9.easy)
items.rewrite: new subject (Fuentes, Dispossessed Lives) replacing Brancusi Bird in Space; no strikingly/colon-list or rather-than clue; key fragmentary pinned by brief mentions

items.passage: Grazing mammals can inadvertently ingest the pea aphids that feed on alfalfa plants. Moshe Gish and colleagues at the University of Haifa found that the aphids detect the elevated heat and humidity of an approaching herbivore’s breath and drop off the plant en masse just before it is eaten, a response that allows most of the colony to ______.
items.stem: Which choice completes the text with the most logical and precise word or phrase?
items.explanation: The aphids drop off the plant “just before it is eaten,” so they are not swallowed along with it. A response that keeps most of the colony from being eaten allows most of the colony to survive.

A.why_wrong: Dropping off the plant is described as a way to avoid being swallowed; the text says nothing about reproduction.

B.why_wrong: The response saves the aphids from being eaten, so saying it allows them to die reverses its effect.

C.why_wrong: The aphids simply drop off the plant; nothing suggests they travel to a new region.

sources.what: Gish, Dafni and Inbar 2010, Current Biology: pea aphids sense the elevated heat and humidity of an approaching herbivore’s breath and salvage most of the colony by dropping off the plant in large numbers immediately before it is eaten
DOI of the paper
University of Haifa team; potted alfalfa eaten by a goat; about 65% of aphids dropped just before they would have been eaten

items.rewrite: new subject (pea aphids flee mammal breath, Gish 2010) replacing Pony Express and telegraph; cause carried by the dropping behavior, no Because clause

items.passage: Ornithologists long regarded singing by female songbirds as ______, treating song as a trait that evolved primarily through competition among males for mates. A 2014 survey led by biologist Karan Odom, however, documented female song in 71 percent of the species examined and concluded that females also sang in the common ancestor of modern songbirds.
items.stem: Which choice completes the text with the most logical and precise word or phrase?
items.explanation: “However” signals that Odom’s finding contrasts with the older view. Odom found female song in 71 percent of the species examined, so the older view must have been that female song was unusual; the first sentence agrees, describing song as treated as a trait shaped by males competing for mates.

A.why_wrong: Widespread is what Odom found; “however” sets her finding against the older view, so the older view cannot also be that female song was widespread.

B.why_wrong: The text never discusses whether song is learned or inborn.

D.why_wrong: Nothing in the text concerns when during the year birds sing.

sources.what: Odom, Hall, Riebel, Omland and Langmore 2014, Nature Communications 5:3379: song historically considered an almost exclusively male trait; female song present in 71% of surveyed species; females sang in the common ancestor of modern songbirds
DOI of the paper
UMBC news on Karan Odom’s Nature Communications paper

items.notes: Theme: natural science (ornithology). Received view then finding, as in 1.27.
items.replaced: Hokusai, Prussian blue and Thirty-six Views of Mount Fuji (duplicate of rhetorical_synthesis.SIM.medium)
items.rewrite: new subject (female birdsong, Odom 2014) replacing Zaha Hadid; contrast via however and the 71 percent finding, no filler opening date

items.passage: Choreographer Michelle Dorrance often treats tap dancers as ______ as well as dancers. In ETM: Double Down, created with Nicholas Van Young, who designed its percussive electronic tap boards, every step triggers a sound, so the performers’ footwork generates the rhythmic loops and melodies of much of the evening’s score.
items.stem: Which choice completes the text with the most logical and precise word or phrase?
items.explanation: The example shows what the dancers do in ETM: Double Down: each step triggers a sound, and their footwork produces the loops and melodies of the score. Dancers who produce a score are acting as musicians as well as dancers.

A.why_wrong: The text credits Van Young with designing the electronic boards; the dancers play the boards, they do not build them.

C.why_wrong: Tap dancing is physical, but the example is about the sounds the dancers produce, not their athletic skill.

D.why_wrong: Nothing in the text says the dancers tell a story; the example concerns sound and the score.

sources.what: ETM: Double Down choreographed by Michelle Dorrance with collaborator Nicholas Van Young; Van Young’s electronic tap boards set off sound with each step; music builds loops from the dancers’ movements
Van Young: about 40 boards act as a gigantic electronic drum set; dancers trigger them to play melodies; “we’re creating the music as we dance”
Electronic tap trigger boards; the entire stage is an instrument; NYT: Dorrance exposes tap’s true nature, that it is music

items.notes: Title italic in print. Theme: arts (dance). An acoustic trio also plays in the show, hence much of the score.
items.rewrite: new subject (Dorrance, ETM: Double Down) replacing the slime-mold Tokyo rail experiment; example pins musicians, no surprisingly hook

items.passage: In experiments by psychologists Juliana Schroeder and Nicholas Epley, evaluators who read transcripts of job candidates’ pitches judged the candidates less ______ than did evaluators who heard the pitches aloud. Listeners rated the speakers as more competent and intelligent and expressed greater interest in hiring them, an effect the researchers traced to vocal cues.
items.stem: Which choice completes the text with the most logical and precise word or phrase?
items.explanation: Listeners rated the speakers as more competent and intelligent and were more interested in hiring them. So evaluators who only read the pitches found the candidates less impressive than listeners did.

B.why_wrong: The ratings described concern competence, intelligence and interest in hiring; honesty is never mentioned.

C.why_wrong: Finding the candidates less dull would mean readers liked them more, but it was the listeners who judged the candidates more favorably.

D.why_wrong: Pitches involve speaking, but the study compared how capable the candidates seemed, not how much they talked.

sources.what: Schroeder and Epley 2015, Psychological Science, The Sound of Intellect: hypothetical employers and professional recruiters rated candidates more competent, thoughtful and intelligent when they heard a pitch rather than read it and were more interested in hiring them; voice conveys intellect
DOI of the paper
APS summary of the study

items.rewrite: new subject (voice and perceived intellect, Schroeder and Epley 2015) replacing hummingbird torpor; negated frame is less ______ than, no record-setting figure

items.passage: Bark scorpion stings cause intense pain in house mice, rats, and humans, yet grasshopper mice routinely prey on the scorpions, grooming only briefly when stung. Ashlee Rowe and colleagues found that these predators are largely ______ the stings: a variant sodium channel in their nerve cells binds the venom’s toxins and blocks the pain signals the venom triggers.
items.stem: Which choice completes the text with the most logical and precise word or phrase?
items.explanation: Grasshopper mice eat the scorpions and groom only briefly when stung, and the venom ends up blocking the pain signals it triggers. Mice that feel little pain from the stings are largely insensitive to them.

A.why_wrong: The mice routinely prey on the scorpions and feel little pain, the opposite of being vulnerable to the stings.

B.why_wrong: The stings protect the scorpions, not the mice; nothing says the mice are protected by them.

D.why_wrong: The scorpions deliver the stings; the mice are not responsible for them.

sources.what: Rowe, Xiao, Rowe, Cummins and Zakon 2013, Science: bark scorpion venom induces pain in house mice, rats and humans; grasshopper mice regularly attack and consume bark scorpions, grooming only briefly when stung; their Nav1.8 variants bind the toxins and block pain signals
DOI of the paper

items.rewrite: new subject (grasshopper mice and bark scorpion venom, Rowe 2013) replacing A Raisin in the Sun; no stacked landmark facts

items.passage:
The following text is from Thomas Hardy’s 1886 novel The Mayor of Casterbridge. Elizabeth-Jane lives in the house of Michael Henchard, a grain and hay merchant who employs Donald Farfrae as his manager.

The position of Elizabeth-Jane’s room—rather high in the house, so that it <u>commanded</u> a view of the hay-stores and granaries across the garden—afforded her opportunity for accurate observation of what went on there. She saw that Donald and Mr. Henchard were inseparables.
items.stem: As used in the text, what does the word “commanded” most nearly mean?
items.explanation: The room is “rather high in the house,” and the result is that Elizabeth-Jane can observe what goes on in the hay-stores and granaries. A high room that “commanded a view” of them is one that offered a view of them.

A.why_wrong: “Command” can mean to give an order, but a room cannot instruct anything.

C.why_wrong: Something can “command” respect or a high price, meaning it earns it, but the room is not earning the view; it simply looks out on the buildings.

D.why_wrong: An officer “commands” troops by leading them, which does not fit a room and a view.

sources.what: Text of The Mayor of Casterbridge (1886), chapter 14, copied from Project Gutenberg

source_updates: source note said chapter 16; the excerpt is in chapter XIV of the Gutenberg text
review.text_check: excerpt matches Gutenberg #143 exactly (chapter XIV); Hardy, 1886, novel, title correct

items.subtype: Most nearly mean: underlined word, phrase options
items.passage:
The following text is from Mark Twain’s 1876 novel The Adventures of Tom Sawyer. As a punishment, Tom’s aunt has made him spend his Saturday whitewashing, or painting, a long fence.

Tom appeared on the sidewalk with a bucket of whitewash and a long-handled brush. He <u>surveyed</u> the fence, and all gladness left him and a deep melancholy settled down upon his spirit. Thirty yards of board fence nine feet high. Life to him seemed hollow, and existence but a burden.
items.stem: As used in the text, what does the word “surveyed” most nearly mean?
items.explanation: Tom has just arrived with his bucket and brush, and the next sentence gives what he sees: “Thirty yards of board fence nine feet high.” Seeing how big the job is makes his gladness leave him, so “surveyed” means took a long look at.

A.why_wrong: To survey people is to poll them, but Tom asks no one anything; he is alone with the fence.

B.why_wrong: Surveyors measure and map land, but Tom is not mapping the fence; he is looking at how much of it he must paint.

C.why_wrong: A survey can be a written overview of a subject, but Tom writes nothing.

sources.what: Text of The Adventures of Tom Sawyer (1876), chapter 2, copied from Project Gutenberg

review.text_check: excerpt matches Gutenberg #74 exactly (chapter II); Twain, 1876, novel, title correct

items.passage: Velvet worms ensnare prey by ejecting a fluid slime that, when mechanically drawn, hardens into stiff biopolymeric fibers. Studying the species Euperipatoides rowelli, a team including Alexander Baer and Matthew Harrington found that this transformation is ______: prolonged immersion in water dissolved the fibers, and regenerated fibers could be drawn from the resulting solution.
items.stem: Which choice completes the text with the most logical and precise word or phrase?
items.explanation: The colon introduces what the team found: water dissolved the hardened fibers, and new fibers could be drawn from the solution. A change that can be undone and then made again is reversible.

A.why_wrong: The fibers dissolved in water and were formed again, so the transformation is not permanent.

B.why_wrong: The slime hardens only “when mechanically drawn,” so the change is triggered, not spontaneous, and the colon is about undoing the change, which spontaneous does not describe.

D.why_wrong: Nothing in the text describes waste; regenerating fibers from dissolved ones reuses the material.

sources.what: Baer, Schmidt, Haensch, Eder, Mayer and Harrington 2017, Nature Communications 8:974, Euperipatoides rowelli: capture slime mechanically drawn into stiff biopolymeric fibres; fibres dissolve with extended exposure to water and regenerated fibres can be drawn from the solution, a fully recyclable process
DOI of the paper
McGill: Matthew Harrington; velvet worm slime captures prey and solidifies into stiff fibers that can dissolve in water and be reformed

items.rewrite: new subject (reversible velvet worm slime fibers, Baer and Harrington 2017) replacing Engel's law; no closing still-refer-to tag; denser register

items.passage: An eleventh-century manuscript known as the Cambridge Songs preserves melodies for poems from Boethius’s Consolation of Philosophy, but only in neumes, signs that indicate melodic direction and details of vocal delivery without specifying every pitch. Musicologist Sam Barrett could thus ______ the songs only by consulting surviving notations in other manuscripts and testing his hypotheses in performance with singer Benjamin Bagby.
items.stem: Which choice completes the text with the most logical and precise word or phrase?
items.explanation: Neumes show melodic direction without specifying every pitch, so the melodies cannot simply be read from the manuscript. Barrett had to rebuild them from notations in other manuscripts and test his hypotheses in performance, which is what it means to reconstruct the songs.

A.why_wrong: Dating is a scholarly task, but the manuscript is already identified as eleventh-century, and the missing pitches explain why the melodies, not the date, were hard to recover.

C.why_wrong: The obstacle described is missing pitch information, which has nothing to do with translating the poems.

D.why_wrong: Nothing in the text concerns who composed the songs; the neumes explain why the melodies had to be worked out.

sources.what: Cambridge University 2016: Cambridge Songs (11th century) leaf with songs from Boethius’s Consolation of Philosophy; neumes indicate melodic direction and details of vocal delivery without specifying every pitch; Barrett gathered surviving notations from other manuscripts; Benjamin Bagby of Sequentia tested the theories in performance; concert at Pembroke College, 23 April 2016
Barrett’s performing edition and the Boethius project at the Cambridge Faculty of Music

items.notes: Title italic in print. Theme: humanities (musicology).
items.rewrite: new subject (Boethius songs from neumes, Sam Barrett) replacing naked mole-rat cancer study; cause carried by thus ... only by, no Because ... concluded chain

items.passage: Kiezdeutsch, a way of speaking that emerged among young people in multilingual urban neighborhoods, is often dismissed as broken German or as immigrants’ failed attempt to speak the standard language. Linguist Heike Wiese contends, however, that its departures from standard German are ______, conforming to grammatical regularities typical of Germanic languages.
items.stem: Which choice completes the text with the most logical and precise word or phrase?
items.explanation: “However” sets Wiese’s view against the claim that Kiezdeutsch is broken German. She says its departures from standard German conform to grammatical regularities, so they are systematic: they follow rules instead of being random errors.

A.why_wrong: Arbitrary departures would be random, which is close to the dismissive view Wiese argues against; following regularities is the opposite.

B.why_wrong: Nothing suggests Kiezdeutsch is a stage on the way to some other form of speech; Wiese’s point concerns its grammar.

C.why_wrong: Cosmetic means surface-level, but the text describes grammatical regularities, a matter of structure, and never says the differences are minor.

sources.what: Review of Wiese, Kiezdeutsch: Ein neuer Dialekt entsteht (Beck 2012): born among youth in multilingual urban environments; Wiese rejects the view that it is broken German or immigrants’ failed attempt at speaking German; it shows systematic grammatical regularities, many typical of Germanic languages
Heike Wiese, linguist; proposal that Kiezdeutsch is a dialect

items.rewrite: new subject (Kiezdeutsch, Heike Wiese) replacing ginkgo aging study; contrast via dismissed ... however, no popular-science hook or three-item list

items.passage: The recent work of multidisciplinary artist Cannupa Hanska Luger is often ______. The installation Every One (2018) began with an instructional video inviting communities across the United States and Canada to make two-inch clay beads; Luger then strung about 4,000 of them, each representing a missing or murdered Indigenous woman or girl, into a monumental portrait.
items.stem: Which choice completes the text with the most logical and precise word or phrase?
items.explanation: The example shows Luger inviting communities across two countries to make the beads that form Every One. Work that depends on the public taking part in its making is participatory.

B.why_wrong: Nothing suggests the work longs for the past; it honors missing and murdered Indigenous women and girls.

C.why_wrong: Beads can be decorative, but the beads in Every One were made by communities to represent people, not to decorate.

D.why_wrong: Insular means closed off from others, the opposite of inviting communities across the United States and Canada to take part.

sources.what: MAD Burke Prize release: Luger is a multidisciplinary artist; for Every One (2018) a video invited communities across the United States and Canada to create and donate two-inch clay beads; each bead is a memorial to one of the four thousand cases; work exemplifies craft as a community endeavor
Ceramics Monthly: each bead represents the life of a missing or murdered Indigenous girl or woman in Canada and the US; beads form an image of a young woman; Luger’s work is built on collaboration
Instructional video launched January 2018 as a call for collaboration; beads strung into a portrait based on Kali Spitzer’s photograph Sister

items.notes: Title italic in print. Theme: arts. Bead counts differ by source (nearly 4,000; more than 4,000; four thousand cases), hence about 4,000.

fixes: “For Every One (2018), his instructional video ...” read as a work titled “For Every One” once italics are lost; now “The installation Every One (2018) began with an instructional video inviting ...” (MAD release: the installation began as an instructional video)

items.rewrite: new subject (Cannupa Hanska Luger, Every One) replacing Gordon Parks; one example pins participatory, no widely celebrated ... remarkably frame

items.passage: Value-added measures of teacher quality, which typically rely solely on students’ standardized test scores, are less ______ than they may appear, according to economist Kirabo Jackson. Analyzing records of North Carolina ninth graders, Jackson found that teachers’ effects on absences, suspensions, and course grades were only weakly correlated with their test-score effects, yet these behavioral effects predicted students’ eventual high school graduation considerably better.
items.stem: Which choice completes the text with the most logical and precise word or phrase?
items.explanation: Jackson found that teachers’ effects on absences, suspensions and grades barely track their effects on test scores, yet predict graduation much better. A measure built only on test scores therefore leaves out an important part of what teachers do: it is less comprehensive than it may appear.

A.why_wrong: Calling the measures less limited than they appear would mean they capture more than expected, but Jackson’s finding shows they miss the behavioral effects that best predict graduation.

B.why_wrong: Nothing in the text concerns whether the measures give the same results when repeated; the finding is about what test scores leave out.

C.why_wrong: The text says nothing about how much debate these measures provoke; it reports what they fail to capture.

sources.what: Jackson, What Do Test Scores Miss? (NBER WP 22226, JPE 2018): extends test-score value-added; teachers affect absences, suspensions, course grades and grade progression; 9th-grade effects predict high-school completion beyond test-score effects

Same paper, full text: North Carolina 9th-grade cohorts; correlations of test-score effects with effects on suspensions and absences below 0.1, with GPA 0.22; 1 SD behavior effect raises graduation 1.47 points vs 0.12 for test-score value-added

Northwestern IPR summary: data on 9th-grade students in North Carolina; non-cognitive effects far more predictive of long-term success in high school; teachers who raise test scores often do not improve behaviors

items.rewrite: New subject (Kirabo Jackson, teacher effects beyond test scores) replacing the famous Vivian Maier story; colon list and round figures gone; denser register; new options and key.

items.subtype: Blank completion: phrase options (article + noun + preposition)
items.passage: Placed in newspapers by enslavers hoping to recapture people who had escaped bondage, the fugitive slave advertisements now compiled in Cornell University’s Freedom on the Move database constitute, paradoxically, ______ resistance to slavery, each one documenting an individual’s flight and frequently describing the person’s appearance, clothing, mannerisms, and speech.
items.stem: Which choice completes the text with the most logical and precise word or phrase?
items.explanation: “Paradoxically” sets the ads’ purpose, helping enslavers recapture people, against what they are now: each one documents a person’s flight from slavery. A collection of documented escapes bears witness to resistance, so the ads are a testament to it.

A.why_wrong: The ads record escapes, but nothing suggests they argue that resisting slavery was justified; they were written by enslavers trying to undo those escapes.

C.recipe: reversal (the trait of the wrong party)
C.why_wrong: Impeding escape was the enslavers’ aim, which is why the text calls the ads’ present role paradoxical; as records of flight, they now bear witness to resistance.

D.why_wrong: Nothing in the text says the ads misinterpret resistance; they simply document individual escapes and describe the people who fled.

sources.what: Freedom on the Move: Cornell-led database of fugitive slave ads placed in newspapers by enslavers trying to locate fugitives; ads include details of appearance, mannerisms, clothing, speech
The ads as records of enslaved people liberating themselves; enslavers placed them to recover people they claimed as property

items.rewrite: New subject (Freedom on the Move fugitive slave ad database) replacing the schoolbook Erie Canal story and its famous quotes; no explanatory since clause; one dense sentence with a participial clue; new options and key.

items.passage:
The following text is from Kate Chopin’s 1897 short story “A Pair of Silk Stockings.” Mrs. Sommers is out shopping.

She carried [her new magazines] without wrapping. As well as she could she lifted her skirts at the crossings. Her stockings and boots and well fitting gloves had worked marvels in her <u>bearing</u>—had given her a feeling of assurance, a sense of belonging to the well-dressed multitude.
items.stem: As used in the text, what does the word “bearing” most nearly mean?
items.explanation: The dash explains what changed in her bearing: the new clothes gave her “a feeling of assurance, a sense of belonging.” That describes how she carries herself and acts, her demeanor.

B.why_wrong: A compass bearing is a direction, but her clothes did not change where she was going.

C.why_wrong: Something can have a bearing on a question, meaning relevance, but that sense has no place in a description of a woman walking in new clothes.

D.why_wrong: To bear something can mean to endure it, but the text describes confidence, not putting up with hardship.

sources.what: Text of “A Pair of Silk Stockings,” in The Awakening, and Selected Short Stories, copied from Project Gutenberg
First published in Vogue, September 16, 1897

items.notes: Bracketed gloss replaces “them” (the magazines bought in the previous sentence), CB style.

review.text_check: excerpt matches Gutenberg #160 exactly apart from the CB-style gloss “[her new magazines]” for “them”; Chopin, 1897 (Vogue), short story, title correct

items.passage:
The following text is from Kate Douglas Wiggin’s 1903 novel Rebecca of Sunnybrook Farm. Rebecca, a young girl, has gotten fresh paint on her best dress and has run to her friends Mrs. Cobb and her husband, Jerry.

Mrs. Cobb <u>took in</u> the situation at a glance, and professed herself able to remove almost any stain from almost any fabric; and in this she was corroborated by uncle Jerry, who vowed that mother could git anything out.
items.stem: As used in the text, what does the phrase “took in” most nearly mean?
items.explanation: Mrs. Cobb took in the situation “at a glance” and at once says she can remove the stain, so in that glance she understood what had happened. “Took in” here means made sense of.

B.why_wrong: To take in a person or animal can mean to give it shelter, but a situation cannot be sheltered.

C.why_wrong: A tailor takes in a dress by making it tighter, but Mrs. Cobb is looking at the situation, not altering the dress.

D.why_wrong: To take someone in can mean to fool them, but Mrs. Cobb is helping, not deceiving anyone.

sources.what: Text of Rebecca of Sunnybrook Farm (1903), chapter 12, copied from Project Gutenberg

items.notes: Excerpt is one complete sentence, copied exactly; “mother” is Jerry’s name for Mrs. Cobb, and the intro names both.

source_updates: source note said chapter 21; the excerpt is in chapter XII (“See the Pale Martyr”) of the Gutenberg text
review.text_check: excerpt matches Gutenberg #498 exactly (chapter XII); Wiggin, 1903, novel, title correct; intro context (paint on her best dress, runs to the Cobbs) matches the preceding text

items.passage: Vietnamese packs considerably more information into an average syllable than Basque does, yet when linguist Christophe Coupé and colleagues compared recordings of speakers of seventeen languages, they found that speech rate tends to ______ such differences in information density. Languages whose syllables carry relatively little information, such as Spanish, were spoken faster than those with information-dense syllables, and all seventeen conveyed information at roughly the same rate.
items.stem: Which choice completes the text with the most logical and precise word or phrase?
items.explanation: The second sentence shows the trade-off: languages with information-light syllables are spoken faster, and all seventeen end up conveying information at about the same rate. Faster speech makes up for less information per syllable, so speech rate tends to offset differences in information density.

A.why_wrong: If speech rate amplified the differences, information-dense languages would also be the fast ones and their rates would pull further apart, but the text says the light languages are faster and the rates come out about equal.

C.why_wrong: “Outpace” suits a text about speed, but the point is not that speech rate moves faster than differences in density; it is that the two balance each other.

D.why_wrong: The text reports that speech rate and information density trade off, not that speech rate determines how much information a language packs into its syllables.

sources.what: Coupé, Oh, Dediu, Pellegrino 2019 (Science Advances): 17 languages, 10 native speakers each reading the same texts; higher speech rates matched by lower information densities (Spanish fast and information-light, Vietnamese and Chinese slower and dense); about 39 bits/s in every language
Paper full text: information density from 4.8 bits per syllable for Basque to 8.0 for Vietnamese; languages more similar in information rate than in density or speech rate

items.rewrite: New subject (Coupé et al. 2019, similar information rates across languages) replacing Granovetter’s weak ties; clue moved to a separate sentence instead of an explanatory colon; new options and key.

items.passage: In a month-long experiment in small factories in Odisha, India, economists Emily Breza, Supreet Kaur, and Yogita Shamdasani found that paying the three workers in a production unit different wages lowered the output of the lowest-paid worker and the attendance even of the highest-paid. Yet where workers could plainly see that better-paid co-workers were more productive, the disparity had no discernible effect: workers apparently objected to pay inequality chiefly when it seemed ______.
items.stem: Which choice completes the text with the most logical and precise word or phrase?
items.explanation: Unequal pay hurt output and attendance except where workers could see that better-paid co-workers really were more productive. Inequality with a visible reason did no harm, so workers objected to it when it seemed unwarranted.

B.why_wrong: Pay differences that seemed merited, backed by visibly higher productivity, are exactly the ones that had no discernible effect.

C.why_wrong: Nothing in the text concerns how long-standing the pay differences were; what decided the effect was whether productivity differences could be seen.

D.why_wrong: Visibility matters in the study, but it is the visibility of co-workers’ productivity that removed the effect; nothing suggests workers objected because the pay gap itself was obvious.

sources.what: Breza, Kaur, Shamdasani, The Morale Effects of Pay Inequality (NBER WP 22491, QJE 2018): month-long experiment, 378 workers in small factories in Odisha; output of workers paid less than both co-workers fell; highest- and median-wage workers in pay-disparity units also had lower attendance; no discernible effect when workers could clearly observe productivity differences; fairness violations only when the rationale for pay differences is unclear; workers sit in three-worker production units, production individual (p. 3)

fixes: “members of a work team” and “teammates” implied joint production; the paper stresses three-worker production units with no joint production (NBER w22491, p. 3), so now “the three workers in a production unit” and “co-workers”

items.rewrite: New subject (Breza, Kaur and Shamdasani pay-inequality experiment) replacing the Jevons paradox; key now needs an inference from the observability result instead of a spelled-out causal chain; new options and key.

items.passage: Some development experts have contended that distributing insecticide-treated bed nets free of charge, rather than at a subsidized price, is ______. Economists Jessica Cohen and Pascaline Dupas found little to support that contention in Kenya. When they randomized the price at which prenatal clinics offered nets to pregnant women, recipients of free nets proved no less likely to use them than women who had paid.
items.stem: Which choice completes the text with the most logical and precise word or phrase?
items.explanation: The evidence that undercuts the contention is that free nets were used as often as paid-for ones, so the contention must have been that free nets would go unused. Giving away nets that people will not use is wasteful.

A.why_wrong: Cost to donors is a real objection to free distribution, but evidence about whether women used their nets says nothing about whether such programs can be funded, so it could not undercut that claim.

C.why_wrong: Finding that free nets are used as much as purchased ones would support the view that free distribution is cost-effective, yet the text says the researchers found little to support the contention.

D.why_wrong: Nothing in the text concerns timing; the study tests whether people who get free nets use them.

sources.what: Cohen and Dupas, Free Distribution or Cost-Sharing? (NBER WP 14406; QJE 2010): it is often argued that cost-sharing is needed to avoid wasting products on people who will not use them; prices randomized at prenatal clinics in Kenya selling ITNs to pregnant women; women who received free nets were not less likely to use them
Published version in the Quarterly Journal of Economics 125(1)

items.passage: Biologists Erik Duboué, Alex Keene, and Richard Borowsky have characterized sleep in the Mexican tetra Astyanax mexicanus as evolutionarily ______. Surface-dwelling populations of the fish sleep roughly thirteen hours a day, for instance, whereas three cave-dwelling populations, each derived independently from surface ancestors after colonizing dark, food-scarce caverns, have all come to sleep only two to four hours.
items.stem: Which choice completes the text with the most logical and precise word or phrase?
items.explanation: The example shows sleep in one species changing drastically, from about thirteen hours to two to four, and doing so separately in three cave populations. A trait that evolution reshapes this readily, and more than once, is malleable.

A.why_wrong: A vestigial trait is a leftover that has lost its function, but nothing in the text suggests sleep has lost its function; the cave fish still sleep, only less.

B.why_wrong: An evolutionarily conserved trait stays much the same across related populations, but sleep in this species differs sharply between surface and cave populations.

D.why_wrong: The amount of sleep did change, but not unpredictably: three populations that colonized similar caves each arrived at the same short sleep.

sources.what: Duboué, Keene, Borowsky 2011, Evolutionary convergence on sleep loss in cavefish populations (Current Biology, DOI 10.1016/j.cub.2011.03.020): dramatic reduction in sleep in three independently derived cave populations; sleep is an evolutionarily labile phenotype
NYU researchers; Pachón, Tinaja and Molino cave populations; surface fish over 800 minutes of sleep a day, cavefish 110 to 250
Surface fish about 13 hours, cavefish 2 to 4 hours; populations lost sleep independently; caves where food is scarce

items.notes: The paper’s own word is “labile”; the key paraphrases it.
items.replaced: English vocabulary borrowed from other languages (duplicate of command_of_evidence.Q1_P3_pairwise.medium)
items.rewrite: New subject (convergent sleep loss in Astyanax cavefish) replacing the textbook four origins of flight; no strikingly opener or colon list; example sentence carries the clue; new options and key.

items.passage: A smudged margin in a late medieval prayer book might be dismissed as mere damage, but for art historian Kathryn Rudy such grime is far from ______. Measuring with a densitometer how much darker certain pages are than others, Rudy has identified the devotional texts that individual readers handled most intensively; one owner, for instance, evidently returned repeatedly to invocations of Saints Sebastian and Adrian, reputed protectors against plague.
items.stem: Which choice completes the text with the most logical and precise word or phrase?
items.explanation: “But” sets Rudy against the view that grime is mere damage, and the next sentence shows her using it as evidence of which prayers readers handled most. Grime that reveals how a book was used is far from extraneous to its study.

A.why_wrong: Rudy uses the grime to identify the prayers readers favored, so it is highly informative; calling it far from informative contradicts the rest of the text.

B.why_wrong: The contrast with “mere damage” might suggest appearance, but the text is about the grime’s value as evidence, not how it looks; a smudged margin is, if anything, unsightly.

D.why_wrong: Nothing in the text concerns whether the damage could be repaired; Rudy measures the grime rather than removing it.

sources.what: Rudy, Dirty Books: Quantifying Patterns of Use in Medieval Manuscripts Using a Densitometer (JHNA 2, 2010): densitometer measures darkness of handled pages as an index of use; in Ms. 128 G 33 the reader heavily used the suffrages to Saints Sebastian and Adrian, two saints thought to ward off the bubonic plague
Rudy argues that cleaning the dirt from such books discards a cultural witness

items.rewrite: New subject (Kathryn Rudy’s densitometer study of grime in prayer books) replacing Gaudí’s hanging-chain model; “far from” frame instead of the borrowed “by no means”; new options and key.

items.passage: Populations of the mosquito Aedes aegypti that strongly prefer human odor to the odor of other animals are concentrated in African regions with intense dry seasons, such as the Sahel. Biologists Noah Rose, Carolyn McBride, and colleagues propose that the species’ predilection for human hosts originally evolved as ______ its reliance on water stored by people, which allows the mosquitoes to breed throughout the protracted dry season.
items.stem: Which choice completes the text with the most logical and precise word or phrase?
items.explanation: Human preference is concentrated where dry seasons are intense, and stored water is what lets the mosquitoes breed through the dry season there. The researchers therefore trace the taste for humans to the reliance on stored water: it originally arose as a by-product of that reliance.

A.why_wrong: An alternative would take the place of the reliance on stored water, but the text finds human preference exactly where mosquitoes depend on stored water; the two go together.

B.why_wrong: Nothing suggests that preferring humans protects mosquitoes from depending on stored water; the text presents that dependence as what lets them breed in the dry season.

C.why_wrong: The text links human preference and reliance on stored water positively, since both occur where dry seasons are intense; nothing suggests the preference gets in the way of that reliance.

sources.what: Rose, ..., McBride 2020, Climate and Urbanization Drive Mosquito Preference for Humans (Current Biology 30(18)): Aedes aegypti from 27 sites in sub-Saharan Africa; preference for human vs animal odor predicted by dry-season intensity and human density; human-biting originally evolved as a by-product of breeding in human-stored water
Strong preference for human hosts only where dry seasons are intense, notably the Sahel, where rainfall is concentrated in a couple of months; dependence on human water storage

items.rewrite: New subject (Aedes aegypti human preference and dry seasons, Rose and McBride 2020) replacing the viral 392-year Greenland shark; no clause that spells the key out; new options and key.

items.passage:
The following text is from Arnold Bennett’s 1908 novel The Old Wives’ Tale. Sophia keeps a boardinghouse in Paris during the 1870–71 siege of the city.

Sophia might have fed her flock without resorting to the official rations, but she would not sacrifice the <u>economy</u> which they represented. She demanded thick clothes for the concierge’s boy, and received boots from Chirac, gloves from Carlier, and a great overcoat from Niepce. The weather increased in severity, and provisions in price.
items.stem: As used in the text, what does the word “economy” most nearly mean?
items.explanation: Sophia could have fed her lodgers (“her flock”) without the rations, but using them is something she will not “sacrifice,” and the last sentence notes that food was getting more expensive. The rations stand for money she keeps, so “economy” here means saving.

A.why_wrong: “The economy” can mean a system of trade and money, but the rations do not represent commerce; they represent what Sophia saves by using them.

B.why_wrong: Economy can mean spareness of style, as in economy of language, which does not fit food rations.

C.why_wrong: An older sense of economy is the management of a household, but the sentence is about what Sophia would lose by not using the rations, which is money, not her control of the house.

sources.what: Text of The Old Wives’ Tale (1908), book 3, copied from Project Gutenberg
Novel first published January 1908; Sophia survives the Siege of Paris running a boarding house

items.rewrite: Intro trimmed to one context sentence (no longer explains the boy and the rations); excerpt, options and key unchanged.
